svg.text: 1 · how does a comparison become a number?
log-odds are a difference of two scores: Bradley–Terry, and an examiner trained to imitate people
2 · how does a score become a gradient?
three lines: fine-tuning on your own answers, each weighted by its score — tied to last week's model by a rope
3 · can we do without the examiner?
DPO: the rope's objective has a closed form; put it back into Bradley–Terry and the examiner drops out
4 · what if the examiner cannot be flattered?
a program checks the answer; answer each question many times and compare within the group (GRPO)
5 · what happens when the examiner is fooled?
people, learned examiners and programs each have a blind spot; one result this week has two explanations

g.text: six parts: a comparison becomes a number → a score becomes a gradient → no examiner (DPO) →
a program as the examiner (RLVR, GRPO) → the examiner is fooled → the bill: sampling plus updating
one sentence for today: “better” comes from an examiner; one score times the gradient of your own answer is the
whole method — and pushed hard enough, the examiner's score and the score you wanted part company.
